                                        Abstract

      We discuss the cone and contraction theorem in a suitable complex analytic
setting. More precisely, we establish the cone and contraction theorem of normal
pairs for projective morphisms between complex analytic spaces. This result is a
starting point of the minimal model program for complex analytic log canonical
pairs. In this book, we are mainly interested in normal pairs whose singularities
are worse than kawamata log terminal singularities. This book is intended to give
a rigorous foundation of the theory of minimal models for projective morphisms of
complex analytic spaces.




     Received by the editor 2023/?/?. This is version 0.00 in 2023/10/9.
     2020 Mathematics Subject Classiﬁcation. Primary 14E30; Secondary 32C15.
     Key words and phrases. minimal model program, log canonical pairs, complex analytic
spaces, cone and contraction theorem, basepoint-free theorem, extremal rational curves, vanishing
theorems, strict support condition.

                                   CHAPTER 1


                                Introduction

     In Section 1.1, we will explain the main results of this book. In Section 1.2, we
will shortly discuss some conjectures on the theory of minimal models for projective
morphisms between complex analytic spaces. In Section 1.3, we will explain some
examples which show various diﬀerences between algebraic varieties and complex
analytic spaces. In Section 1.4, we will describe the contents of each chapter more
precisely for the reader’s convenience.


                                1.1. Main results
     In his epoch-making paper [Mo], Shigefumi Mori established the cone theorem
for smooth projective varieties deﬁned over any algebraically closed ﬁeld k of arbi-
trary characteristic by his ingenious method of bend and break. Then he established
the contraction theorem for smooth projective threefolds when the characteristic
of the base ﬁeld k is zero. After that, in characteristic zero, the cone and contrac-
tion theorem was generalized for so-called log-terminal pairs in any dimension by
using Hironaka’s resolution of singularities and the Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing
theorem. For the details, see [KMM], [KM], [Ma] and references therein. Now
we know that, in characteristic zero, the cone and contraction theorem holds for
more general settings (see [Fu3], [Fu5, Chapter 6], [Fu9], and references therein).
In this book, we will discuss the cone and contraction theorem of normal pairs for
projective morphisms between complex analytic spaces. For kawamata log terminal
pairs, it was known and has played an important role in [Na1], [Na2], and [Fu11].
In [Fu11], we have already discussed the minimal model program for kawamata log
terminal pairs in a complex analytic setting (see also [Fu16]). Roughly speaking,
we showed that [BCHM] and [HM2] can work for projective morphisms between
complex analytic spaces. We note that the Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing theorem
can be formulated and proved for projective morphisms of complex analytic spaces
and is suﬃcient for the study of kawamata log terminal pairs. We also note that
L2 -methods can work for kawamata log terminal pairs. For an alternative approach
to the minimal model program of kawamata log terminal pairs for projective mor-
phisms between complex analytic spaces, see [DHP], which uses the idea of [CL].
The reader can ﬁnd a new approach to the relative minimal model program in
[LM], which can work in larger categories of spaces. In [Fu13], we established
some vanishing theorems and related results necessary for the study of complex
analytic log canonical pairs and quasi-log structures on complex analytic spaces.

    Theorem 1.1.1 ([Fu13, Theorem 1.1], see also Theorem 3.1.5). Let (X, ∆) be
an analytic simple normal crossing pair such that ∆ is a boundary R-divisor on X.
Let f : X → Y be a projective morphism to a complex analytic space Y and let L
                                          1
2                                 1. INTRODUCTION


be a line bundle on X. Let q be an arbitrary non-negative integer. Then we have
the following properties.
       (i) (Strict support condition). If L − (ωX + ∆) is f -semiample, then every
           associated subvariety of Rq f∗ L is the f -image of some stratum of (X, ∆).
      (ii) (Vanishing theorem). If L − (ωX + ∆) ∼R f ∗ H holds for some π-ample
           R-line bundle H on Y , where π : Y → Z is a projective morphism to a
           complex analytic space Z, then we have
                                  R p π∗ R q f ∗ L = 0
         for every p > 0.
    Note that [Fu13] depends on Morihiko Saito’s theory of mixed Hodge mod-
ules (see [Sa1], [Sa2], [Sa3], [FFS], and [Sa4]) and Takegoshi’s generalization of
Kollár’s torsion-free and vanishing theorem (see [Ta]). For an approach to Theorem
1.1.1 without using the theory of mixed Hodge modules, see [FF], where we use the
theory of variations of mixed Hodge structure. As in the algebraic case (see [Fu3]
and [Fu5]), our philosophy is as follows.
    1.1.2 (Philosophy). From the Hodge theoretic viewpoint, we have the following
correspondences.
          Kawamata log terminal pairs        ⇐⇒          Pure Hodge structures
and
                Quasi-log pairs     ⇐⇒       Mixed Hodge structures

    In this book, we will discuss the cone and contraction theorem of normal pairs
for projective morphisms between complex analytic spaces as an application of
Theorem 1.1.1. More generally, in [Fu14], we will discuss quasi-log structures for
complex analytic spaces. We can see this book as a complex analytic generaliza-
tion of [Fu3] and as a generalization of Nakayama’s paper [Na1]. We note that
Nakayama only treated kawamata log terminal pairs and Q-divisors in [Na1]. Fi-
nally, the main part of this book is independent of [Fu11] and does not use any
results obtained in [Fu11].
    This book is intended to give a rigorous foundation of the theory of minimal
models for projective morphisms of complex analytic spaces.
     1.1.3 (Standard setting). One of the main diﬃculties to discuss the minimal
model theory for complex analytic spaces is how to formulate it.
     Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism between complex analytic spaces such
that X is a normal complex variety and let W be a compact subset of Y . In this
book, we formulate and prove almost everything over some open neighborhood of
W . Let ∆ be an R-divisor on X such that KX + ∆ is R-Cartier. The number
of the irreducible components of Supp ∆ is only locally ﬁnite. In general, the
support of ∆ may have inﬁnitely many irreducible components. By shrinking Y
around W suitably, that is, by replacing Y with a suitable relatively compact open
neighborhood of W , we can always assume that Supp ∆ has only ﬁnitely many
irreducible components. Moreover, we can assume that a given R-Cartier divisor
on X is a ﬁnite R-linear combination of Cartier divisors. Therefore, by considering
some relatively compact open neighborhood of W , we can avoid subtle problems
caused by the diﬀerence between the Zariski topology and the Euclidean topology.
                                 1.1. MAIN RESULTS                                   3


In [Fu11], we almost always assume that W is a Stein compact subset of Y such that
Γ(W, OY ) is noetherian. In this book, however, we usually assume that W is only
a compact subset of Y . When we consider the Kleiman–Mori cone NE(X/Y ; W ) of
π : X → Y and W , we further assume that the dimension of N 1 (X/Y ; W ) is ﬁnite.
For the details of NE(X/Y ; W ) and N 1 (X/Y ; W ), see Section 4.4. Note that if
W ∩V has only ﬁnitely many connected components for any analytic subset V which
is deﬁned over an open neighborhood of W then the dimension of N 1 (X/Y ; W ) is
ﬁnite by Nakayama’s ﬁniteness (see Theorem 4.5.2). Therefore, if W is a compact
semianalytic subset of Y , then the dimension of N 1 (X/Y ; W ) is always ﬁnite. Thus,
we can ﬁnd many compact subsets W with dimR N 1 (X/Y ; W ) < ∞.
    Although we are mainly interested in normal complex varieties in this book,
we frequently have to treat disjoint unions of normal complex varieties.
     Remark 1.1.4. Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism from a normal com-
plex variety X to a complex analytic space Y and let W be a compact subset of
Y as in 1.1.3. Throughout this book, we frequently shrink Y around W . More
precisely, we replace Y with an open neighborhood U of W . If the natural map
OY → π∗ OX is an isomorphism, then π −1 (U ) is connected for every connected
open subset U of Y . However, if general ﬁbers of π : X → Y are not connected,
then π −1 (U ) may become a disjoint union of normal complex varieties even when
U is connected. Moreover, if π is surjective and U is not connected, then π −1 (U )
is obviously a disjoint union of normal complex varieties.

    Main theorem: In this book, we call (X, ∆) a normal pair if it consists of a
normal complex variety X and an eﬀective R-divisor ∆ on X such that KX + ∆
is R-Cartier. The main purpose of this book is to establish the following cone and
contraction theorem of normal pairs for projective morphisms between complex
analytic spaces.
    Theorem 1.1.5 (Main theorem, cone and contraction theorem, see Theorems
4.6.1, 4.6.2, 5.1.2, and 5.2.4). Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism of complex
analytic spaces such that X is a normal complex variety and let W be a compact
subset of Y . Assume that the dimension of N 1 (X/Y ; W ) is ﬁnite. Let ∆ be an
eﬀective R-divisor on X such that KX + ∆ is R-Cartier. Then we have
                                                                        X
     NE(X/Y ; W ) = NE(X/Y ; W )(KX +∆)≥0 + NE(X/Y ; W )Nlc(X,∆) +          Rj
with the following properties.
     (1) Nlc(X, ∆) is the non-lc locus of (X, ∆) and NE(X/Y ; W )Nlc(X,∆) is the
         subcone of NE(X/Y ; W ) which is the closure of the convex cone spanned
         by the projective integral curves C on Nlc(X, ∆) such that π(C) is a point
         of W .
     (2) Rj is a (KX + ∆)-negative extremal ray of NE(X/Y ; W ) which satisﬁes
                         Rj ∩ NE(X/Y ; W )Nlc(X,∆) = {0}
         for every j.
     (3) Let A be a π-ample R-line bundle on X. Then there are only ﬁnitely
         many Rj ’s included in NE(X/Y ; W )(KX +∆+A)<0 . In particular, the Rj ’s
         are discrete in the half-space NE(X/Y ; W )(KX +∆)<0 .
4                                1. INTRODUCTION


     (4) Let F be any face of NE(X/Y ; W ) such that
                                                          
          F ∩ NE(X/Y ; W )(KX +∆)≥0 + NE(X/Y ; W )Nlc(X,∆) = {0}.
         Then, after shrinking Y around W suitably, there exists a contraction
         morphism ϕF : X → Z over Y satisfying the following properties.
           (i) Let C be a projective integral curve on X such that π(C) is a point of
               W . Then ϕF (C) is a point if and only if the numerical equivalence
               class [C] of C is in F .
          (ii) The natural map OZ → (ϕF )∗ OX is an isomorphism.
         (iii) Let L be a line bundle on X such that L · C = 0 for every curve
               C with [C] ∈ F . Then, after shrinking Y around W suitably again,
               there exists a line bundle LZ on Z such that L ≃ ϕ∗F LZ holds.
     (5) Every (KX + ∆)-negative extremal ray R with
                         R ∩ NE(X/Y ; W )Nlc(X,∆) = {0}
         is spanned by a (possibly singular) rational curve C with
                          0 < −(KX + ∆) · C ≤ 2 dim X.
    From now on, we further assume that (X, ∆) is log canonical, equivalently,
Nlc(X, ∆) = ∅. Then we have the following properties.
     (6) Let H be an eﬀective R-Cartier R-divisor on X such that KX + ∆ + H is
         π-nef over W and (X, ∆ + H) is log canonical. Then, either KX + ∆ is
         also π-nef over W or there exists a (KX + ∆)-negative extremal ray R of
         NE(X/Y ; W ) such that
                             (KX + ∆ + λH) · R = 0,
         where
                 λ := inf{t ≥ 0 | KX + ∆ + tH is π-nef over W }.
          Of course, KX + ∆ + λH is π-nef over W .
Similarly, we have:
     (7) Let H be an R-line bundle on X which is π-ample over W such that
          KX + ∆ + H is π-nef over W . Then, either KX + ∆ is also π-nef over
          W or there exists a (KX + ∆)-negative extremal ray R of NE(X/Y ; W )
          such that
                             (KX + ∆ + λH) · R = 0,
          where
                 λ := inf{t ≥ 0 | KX + ∆ + tH is π-nef over W }.
         Note that KX + ∆ + λH is π-nef over W .
    Remark 1.1.6. In Theorem 1.1.5, the proof of (5) needs Mori’s bend and
break method and (6) is an application of (5). On the other hand, (7) is an easy
consequence of (3). Note that π-very ample line bundles do not always have global
sections. Hence (7) is not a special case of (6). We need (7) in order to discuss
the minimal model program of log canonical pairs with ample scaling for projective
morphisms between complex analytic spaces.
    For the minimal model program, the following theorem, which is a supplement
to Theorem 1.1.5, may be useful (see [Fu11]).
                                  1.1. MAIN RESULTS                                    5


    Theorem 1.1.7. Let (X, ∆) be a log canonical pair. Let π : X → Y be a
projective morphism of complex analytic spaces and let W be a compact subset of
Y such that the dimension of N 1 (X/Y ; W ) is ﬁnite. Suppose that π : X → Y is
decomposed as
                               π: X
                                        f
                                            / Y♭   g
                                                       /Y
such that Y is projective over Y . Let AY ♭ be a g-ample line bundle on Y ♭ . Let R be
            ♭

a (KX + ∆ + (dim X + 1)f ∗ AY ♭ )-negative extremal ray of NE(X/Y ; W ). Then R
is a (KX +∆)-negative extremal ray of NE X/Y ♭ ; g −1 (W ) , that is, R·f ∗ AY ♭ = 0.
     We prove Theorem 1.1.7 as an application of the vanishing theorem for projec-
tive quasi-log schemes. We do not need Theorem 1.1.5 (5) for the proof of Theorem
1.1.7. We have the following result as an easy consequence of Theorem 1.1.7.
    Corollary 1.1.8 (see [Fu8, Corollary 1.2]). Let (X, ∆) be a log canonical
pair. Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism of complex analytic spaces and let
A be any π-ample line bundle on X. Then KX + ∆ + (dim X + 1)A is always nef
over Y .
    We make an important remark on Theorem 1.1.5. By Remark 1.1.9, we see that
the cone and contraction theorem of normal pairs holds for projective morphisms
between compact analytic spaces.
     Remark 1.1.9. Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism of complex analytic
spaces and let W be a compact subset of Y as in Theorem 1.1.5. Then the dimen-
sion of N 1 (X/Y ; W ) is not always ﬁnite (see Example 4.5.1). In [Na2, Chapter
II. 5.19. Lemma] (see Theorem 4.5.2), Noboru Nakayama proved that if
         • W is a compact subset of Y such that W ∩ V has only ﬁnitely many
           connected components for any analytic subset V which is deﬁned over an
           open neighborhood of W ,
then the dimension of N 1 (X/Y ; W ) is ﬁnite. We note that the above assumption
is satisﬁed in the following cases:
       (i) W is a point of Y .
      (ii) W is a compact semianalytic subset of Y .
     (iii) W = Y when Y is compact.
Case (i) is obvious. In Case (ii), W ∩V is a compact semianalytic subset of Y . Thus
we see that W ∩ V has only ﬁnitely many connected components (see, for example,
[BM1, Corollary 2.7 (2)]). In Case (iii), W ∩ V = V is a compact analytic subset
of Y . Hence it has only ﬁnitely many connected components.
     By Remark 1.1.9, we see that there are many compact subsets W of Y such
that the dimension of N 1 (X/Y ; W ) is ﬁnite.
     We note that we can formulate and prove the basepoint-free theorem for pro-
jective morphisms of complex analytic spaces as follows. In Theorem 1.1.10, L is
only assumed to be π-nef over W , that is, L|π−1 (w) is nef in the usual sense for every
w ∈ W . Equivalently, L · C ≥ 0 for every projective integral curve C on X such
that π(C) is a point of W . However, Theorem 1.1.10 claims that it is π-semiample
over some open neighborhood of W .
    Theorem 1.1.10 (Basepoint-free theorem: Theorem 4.2.1). Let π : X → Y be
a projective morphism of complex analytic spaces such that X is a normal complex
6                                1. INTRODUCTION


variety and let W be a compact subset of Y . Let ∆ be an eﬀective R-divisor on X
such that KX + ∆ is R-Cartier. Let L be a Cartier divisor on X which is π-nef
over W . We assume that
      (i) aL − (KX + ∆) is π-ample over W for some positive real number a, and
     (ii) there exists some open neighborhood of W over which ONlc(X,∆) (mL) is
          π|Nlc(X,∆) -generated for every m ≫ 0.
Then there exists a relatively compact open neighborhood U of W such that OX (mL)
is π-generated over U for every m ≫ 0.
    In Theorem 1.1.10, W is only assumed to be a compact subset of Y . We do
not need the assumption that dimR N 1 (X/Y ; W ) < ∞ holds. When (X, ∆) is log
canonical, we will also prove the basepoint-free theorem for R-Cartier divisors.
     Theorem 1.1.11 (Basepoint-free theorem for R-divisors, see Theorem 5.3.1).
Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism of complex analytic spaces such that X is a
normal complex variety and let W be a compact subset of Y such that the dimension
of N 1 (X/Y ; W ) is ﬁnite. Let ∆ be an eﬀective R-divisor on X such that (X, ∆) is
log canonical. Let D be an R-Cartier R-divisor deﬁned on some open neighborhood
of π −1 (W ) such that D is π-nef over W . Assume that aD − (KX + ∆) is π-ample
over W for some positive real number a. Then there exists an open neighborhood
U of W such that D is semiample over U .
    In Theorem 1.1.11, we have to assume that the dimension of N 1 (X/Y ; W ) is
ﬁnite since we need the cone theorem for the proof of Theorem 5.3.1. In the proof
of Theorems 1.1.5, 1.1.10, and so on, the following basic properties of log canonical
centers play an important role.
    Theorem 1.1.12 (Basic properties of log canonical centers: Theorem 3.4.1).
Let (X, ∆) be a log canonical pair. Then the following properties hold.
     (1) The number of log canonical centers of (X, ∆) is locally ﬁnite.
     (2) The intersection of two log canonical centers is a union of some log canon-
         ical centers.
     (3) Let x ∈ X be any point such that (X, ∆) is log canonical but is not kawa-
         mata log terminal at x. Then there exists a unique minimal (with respect
         to the inclusion) log canonical center Cx passing through x. Moreover, Cx
         is normal at x.
    Theorem 1.1.12 is new for complex analytic log canonical pairs although it is
well known when (X, ∆) is algebraic. It will be useful for the study of complex
analytic log canonical singularities (see also [Fu12]).
    Theorem 1.1.5 is a starting point of the minimal model program of log canonical
pairs for projective morphisms between complex analytic spaces. We can formulate
the minimal model theory of log canonical pairs for projective morphisms between
complex analytic spaces by using Theorem 1.1.5 as in the algebraic case. Here,
we only explain one of the main goals of the minimal model theory for projective
morphisms between complex analytic spaces.
    Conjecture 1.1.13 (Finite generation). Let π : X → Y be a projective mor-
phism of complex analytic spaces and let ∆ be an eﬀective Q-divisor on X such that
(X, ∆) is log canonical. Then
                                       M
                  R(X/Y, KX + ∆) :=        π∗ OX (⌊m(KX + ∆)⌋)
                                       m∈N
                         1.2. MINIMAL MODEL CONJECTURE                               7


is a locally ﬁnitely generated graded OY -algebra.
    We note that in [Fu11] Conjecture 1.1.13 was already solved completely when
(X, ∆) is kawamata log terminal. We also note that Conjecture 1.1.13 is still widely
open even when π : X → Y is algebraic (see [FG]). For some other conjectures, see
Section 1.2.
    The author ﬁrst prepared a short manuscript which only explains how to modify
arguments in [Fu3]. Unfortunately, however, it seemed to be hard to read. Hence
he made great eﬀorts to make this book as self-contained as possible except for
the results established in [Fu13] (see also [Fu15] and [FF]). He sometimes repeats
arguments in [Fu3] and [Fu5]. Thus, some parts of this book are very similar to
those of [Fu3] and [Fu5].
    Remark 1.1.14 (Quasi-log structures, see Section 6.1). By [Fu13, Theorems
1.1 and 1.2] (see Theorems 3.1.5 and 3.2.3), we can formulate and discuss quasi-
log structures on complex analytic spaces (see [Fu5, Chapter 6]). Hence we can
establish the cone and contraction theorem for highly singular complex analytic
spaces. However, in this book, we will only discuss the cone and contraction theorem
of normal pairs (see Theorem 1.1.5). This is because Theorem 1.1.5 is suﬃcient for
many geometric applications and it is not so easy psychologically to treat reducible
complex analytic spaces. We will describe the theory of quasi-log complex analytic
spaces in [Fu14] (see also Sections 6.1, 6.2, and 6.3). By using the theory of
quasi-log complex analytic spaces, we will establish the basepoint-free theorem of
Reid–Fukuda type (see Theorem 6.2.1), the eﬀective freeness (see Theorems 6.3.1
and 6.3.2), and the eﬀective very ampleness (see Theorem 6.3.3) in [Fu14]. Finally,
the theory of quasi-log structures seems to be useful for the study of rational chain
connectedness (see Section 6.5).
    In this book, every complex analytic space is assumed to be Hausdorﬀ and
second-countable. An irreducible and reduced complex analytic space is called a
complex variety. We will freely use the standard notation in [Fu3], [Fu5], [Fu11],
and so on. We will also freely use the basic results on complex analytic geometry
in [BS] and [Fi]. For the minimal model program for projective morphisms be-
tween complex analytic spaces, see [Na1], [Na2], and [Fu11]. For the traditional
framework of the minimal model program, see [KMM], [KM], and [Ma]. We note
that Z, Q, and R denote the set of integers, rational numbers, and real numbers,
respectively. We also note that N (resp. Z>0 ) is the set of non-negative integers
(resp. positive integers).

                        1.2. Minimal model conjecture
     In this section, we will discuss the minimal model conjecture for projective
morphisms between complex analytic spaces. Here, we will not treat the minimal
model program of complex analytic spaces systematically (see [Fu11]). We will only
explain some conjectures related to the theory of minimal models in the complex
analytic setting. For some related results, see Section 6.4. Let us start with the
following important and diﬃcult conjecture.
     Conjecture 1.2.1. Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism of complex ana-
lytic spaces, let (X, ∆) be a log canonical pair, and let W be a compact subset of Y .
Assume that KX + ∆ is π-nef over W , that is, (KX + ∆) · C ≥ 0 holds for every
8                                 1. INTRODUCTION


projective integral curve C on X such that π(C) is a point of W . Then KX + ∆ is
nef over some open neighborhood U of W .
    Let us recall the deﬁnition of small projective morphisms in order to explain
ﬂips.
    Definition 1.2.2 (Small projective morphisms). Let ϕ : X → Z be a projective
morphism of normal complex varieties. If the exceptional locus of ϕ has codimension
≥ 2, then ϕ is called small.
   The existence of log canonical ﬂips is still open in the complex analytic setting.
Note that Conjecture 1.2.3 holds true in the usual algebraic setting.
    Conjecture 1.2.3 (Flip conjecture I). Let ϕ : X → Z be a small projective
morphism of complex analytic spaces and let (X, ∆) be a log canonical pair. Assume
that −(KX + ∆) is ϕ-ample. Then we can construct the following commutative
diagram:
                          (X, ∆) _ _ _ _ _ _ _/ (X + , ∆+ )
                                        ϕ
                               EE
                                 EE               uu
                                   EE          uuu
                                  φ EE        u
                                       E" zuuu φ+
                                         Z
where
       (i) (X + , ∆+ ) is log canonical,
      (ii) ϕ+ : X + → Z is small projective, and
     (iii) KX + + ∆+ is ϕ+ -ample, where ∆+ is the strict transform of ∆ on X + .
We call ϕ+ : (X + , ∆+ ) → Z a (KX + ∆)-ﬂip of ϕ. The exceptional locus of ϕ
(resp. ϕ+ ) is called the ﬂipping (resp. ﬂipped) locus. We note that we frequently
simply say that φ : X 99K X + is a ﬂip if there is no danger of confusion. Fur-
thermore, if Z is projective over a complex analytic space Y , then we say that
φ : X 99K X + is a ﬂip over Y .
    If (X, ∆) is a kawamata log terminal pair, then we know that Conjecture 1.2.3
holds true (see [Fu11]). The termination of ﬂips is one of the most diﬃcult open
problems.
      Conjecture 1.2.4 (Flip conjecture II). Let (X, ∆) be a log canonical pair and
let
                                ϕ0            ϕ1     ϕi−1          ϕi
           (X, ∆) =: (X0 , ∆0 ) 99K (X1 , ∆1 ) 99K · · · 99K (Xi , ∆i ) 99K · · ·
be a sequence of ﬂips over a complex analytic space Y starting from (X, ∆). Let W
be a compact subset of Y . Then, there exists some i0 such that φi is an isomorphism
over W for every i ≥ i0 , that is, φi is an isomorphism over some open neighborhood
Ui of W for every i ≥ i0 .
    Conjecture 1.2.4 is still widely open even when everything is algebraic. The
abundance conjecture is also a very diﬃcult open problem. It is also widely open
even for projective varieties.
    Conjecture 1.2.5 (Abundance conjecture). Let π : X → Y be a projective
morphism of complex analytic spaces, let (X, ∆) be a log canonical pair, and let W
be a compact subset of Y . Assume that KX + ∆ is π-nef over W . Then KX + ∆
is π-semiample over some open neighborhood U of W .
                            1.3. ALGEBRAIC VS ANALYTIC                               9


     The ﬁnite generation of log canonical rings for log canonical pairs is an im-
portant open problem. For the details of Conjecture 1.2.6 for the case where
π : (X, ∆) → Y is algebraic, see [FG].
     Conjecture 1.2.6 (Finite generation, see Conjecture 1.1.13). Let π : X → Y
be a projective morphism of complex analytic spaces and let ∆ be an eﬀective Q-
divisor on X such that (X, ∆) is log canonical. Then
                                       M
                 R(X/Y, KX + ∆) :=        π∗ OX (⌊m(KX + ∆)⌋)
                                        m∈N
is a locally ﬁnitely generated graded OY -algebra.
    If (X, ∆) is a kawamata log terminal pair, then we know that Conjecture 1.2.6
holds true (see [Fu11] and Theorem 6.4.1). If (X, ∆) is log canonical but is not
kawamata log terminal, then Conjecture 1.2.6 is open even when π : (X, ∆) → Y is
algebraic. For the details of the theory of minimal models of kawamata log terminal
pairs for projective morphisms between complex analytic spaces, see [Fu11].

                           1.3. Algebraic vs Analytic
     In this section, we will see various diﬀerences between algebraic varieties and
complex analytic spaces for the reader’s convenience. The reader can ﬁnd some
interesting examples in [Sh, Chapter 8, Sections 1.4, 3.2, and 3.3].
     Let X be an algebraic variety. Then we can always take a completion X ,→ X,
that is, X is a complete algebraic variety which contains X as a Zariski open dense
subset of X. If X 1 and X 2 are two diﬀerent completions of X, then it is obvious that
X 1 is birationally equivalent to X 2 by deﬁnition. Unfortunately, a complex analytic
space is not always compactiﬁable. Moreover, two diﬀerent compactiﬁcations of a
given complex manifold are not necessarily bimeromorphically equivalent. Let us
recall the following famous example due to Serre.
     Example 1.3.1 (Serre, see [Ha, Chapter VII, Example 3.2]). Let C be an
elliptic curve and let E be the rank two vector bundle on C which is deﬁned by the
unique non-splitting extension
                               0 → OC → E → O C → 0
We consider the ruled surface X := PC (E). On that surface there exists a unique
section
                                 D := PC (OC ) ⊂ X
of X → C such that OD (D) ≃ OD holds and that OX (D) ≃ OPC (E) (1) is a nef
line bundle on X. We put U := X \ D. Then U is obviously a quasi-projective
algebraic surface. We can easily check that U is not aﬃne. Let U an be the complex
analytic space naturally associated to U . Then we can check that U an is analytically
isomorphic to C× × C× , where C× = C \ {0}. In particular, U an is a Stein manifold.
This example shows that the complex analytic space C× × C× has two diﬀerent
compactiﬁcations as follows:
                                                     
                    X = P (E) o
                           C
                                       ? _ C× × C×    / P1 × P1 .

Note that X is not bimeromorphically equivalent to P1 × P1 .
   Here we recall the precise deﬁnition of bimeromorphic maps for the sake of
completeness.
10                               1. INTRODUCTION


     Definition 1.3.2 (Bimeromorphic maps). A meromorphic map f : X 99K Y of
complex analytic varieties is deﬁned by the graph Γf ⊂ X × Y such that Γf is a
subvariety of X × Y and that the ﬁrst projection is proper and is an isomorphism
over a Zariski open dense subset of X. Note that a Zariski open subset is the
complement of an analytic subset. If further the second projection Γf → Y is proper
and is an isomorphism over a Zariski open dense subset of Y , then f : X 99K Y is
called a bimeromorphic map. If there exists a bimeromprhic map between X and
Y , then we say that X is bimeromorphically equivalent to Y .
                                                                  ∼
     In Example 1.3.1, the graph of the analytic isomorphism U −→ C× × C× can
not be extended to a closed subvariety of X × (P1 × P1 ). This is the reason why X
is not bimeromorphically equivalent to P1 × P1 .
     Let L be a line bundle on an algebraic variety X. Then we can always ﬁnd
a Cartier divisor D on X such that L ≃ OX (D). This property does not always
hold for complex analytic varieties. A simplest example, which is due to Siegel, is
as follows.
    Example 1.3.3 (Complex tori). Let T be a two-dimensional complex torus
with a period matrix                     √      √ 
                                  1 0 √−2 √−5
                           Ω=                           .
                                  0 1       −3     −7
Then it is well known that it has no non-constant meromorphic functions. Of
course, the algebraic dimension of T is zero and there are no one-dimensional closed
subvarieties on T .
    Note that there are many compact complex manifolds which have no non-
constant meromorphic functions. In this book, we are mainly interested in non-
compact complex analytic spaces. We have to take care of the following simple
example. For a related topic, see [Fu12].
     Example 1.3.4 (Q-Cartier Q-divisors). Let {Pn }n∈Z>0 be a set of mutually
distinct discrete points of X := C. Then
                                      X n−1
                                ∆ :=          Pn
                                           n
                                     n∈Z>0

is a Q-Cartier Q-divisor on a complex manifold X. In this case, there is no positive
integer m such that m∆ is Cartier. We note that (X, ∆) is kawamata log terminal.
However, (X, t∆) is not log canonical for every t > 1.
    If we apply Theorem 1.1.10, which is the basepoint-free theorem, to the usual
algebraic setting, we have the following basepoint-free theorem, which is related to
Conjecture 1.2.1.
    Theorem 1.3.5. Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism of quasi-projective
algebraic varieties such that (X, ∆) is log canonical. Let P ∈ Y be a closed point.
Let L be a Cartier divisor on X such that L · C ≥ 0 holds for every projective
integral curve C on X with π(C) = P . Assume that aL − (KX + ∆) is π-ample
for some positive real number a. Then there exists a Zariski open neighborhood U
of P such that OX (mL) is π-generated over U for every m ≫ 0. In particular, L
is π-nef over U .
     We prove Theorem 1.3.5 for the sake of completeness.
                              1.4. PRECISE CONTENTS                                11


    Proof of Theorem 1.3.5. By Theorem 1.1.10, we can take positive integers
m1 and m2 such that (m1 , m2 ) = 1 and that OX (m1 L) and OX (m2 L) are π-
generated over an open neighborhood U ′ of P . We note that
                   Si := π (Supp(π ∗ π∗ OX (mi L) → OX (mi L)))
is a closed analytic subset of Y which is disjoint from U ′ for i = 1, 2. We put
                                             [
                                 U := Y \        Si .
                                           i=1,2

Then we can easily see that this U is a desired Zariski open neighborhood of P .   
     Note that L is not assumed to be π-nef in Theorem 1.3.5. We only assumed
that L is π-nef over P . Therefore, Theorem 1.3.5 is new even when π : (X, ∆) → Y
is algebraic. The ﬁnal example in this section is more or less well known.
    Example 1.3.6 (see, for example, [Fu1, Example 3.2.4]). We consider
                 X := {(x, y, z, w) ∈ C4 | xy + zw + z 3 + w3 = 0}.
Then X is a Q-factorial aﬃne algebraic variety, that is, every prime divisor on X
is Q-Cartier. More precisely, the coordinate ring
                         C[x, y, z, w]/(xy + zw + z 3 + w3 )
of X is a UFD. Let us consider a germ of X an around the origin, where X an is
the complex analytic space associated to X. It is easy to see that X an is local
analytically isomorphic to (xy − uv = 0) ⊂ C4 around the origin. The two divisors
(x = u = 0) and (y = v = 0) intersect at a single point. Hence, on a germ of X an ,
there exists a prime divisor which is not Q-Cartier at the origin.
   By Example 1.3.6, we see that the notion of Q-factoriality is subtle for normal
complex varieties.

                              1.4. Precise contents
    In this section, we will describe the contents of each chapter more precisely for
the reader’s convenience.
     Chapter 2: Chapter 2 is a preliminary chapter. In Section 2.1, we collect some
necessary deﬁnitions and results for the reader’s convenience. Since we have to work
in the complex analytic setting, some of them become much more subtle than the
usual ones in the algebraic setting. In Section 2.2, we collect some basic properties
of relatively nef and relatively ample R-line bundles for the sake of completeness.
They are indispensable in subsequent sections. We note that we have to treat R-
line bundles in the theory of minimal models. In Section 2.3, we deﬁne non-lc ideal
sheaves in the complex analytic setting and prove some elementary lemmas.
    Chapter 3: Chapter 3 is devoted to our new vanishing theorems in the complex
analytic setting established in [Fu13] and their direct consequences. In Section 3.1,
we quickly recall the main result of [Fu13] without proof. Note that the proof of
the main result in [Fu13] depends on Saito’s theory of mixed Hodge modules and
Takegoshi’s generalization of Kollár’s torsion-free and vanishing theorem. However,
we can make the main result of [Fu13] free from the theory of mixed Hodge modules
by [FF]. Section 3.2 is a short section, where we treat vanishing theorems of Reid–
Fukuda type. We note that we do not need them in this book. In Section 3.3, we
12                                1. INTRODUCTION


prove some vanishing theorems for normal pairs as applications of the vanishing
result explained in Section 3.1. In Section 3.4, we establish the basic properties of
log canonical centers. They are new and very important in the theory of minimal
models in the complex analytic setting.

     Chapter 4: Chapter 4 is the main part of this book. Here we establish the
fundamental theorems of the theory of minimal models for projective morphisms
between complex analytic spaces. In Section 4.1, we prove the non-vanishing theo-
rem in the complex analytic setting with the aid of the theory of quasi-log schemes.
Note that Lemma 4.1.2 is new and will be useful for the study of quasi-log struc-
tures. In Section 4.2, we establish the basepoint-free theorem for normal pairs in
the complex analytic setting by using the non-vanishing theorem proved in Section
4.1. It is well known and is not diﬃcult to prove for kawamata log terminal pairs.
In Sections 4.3, we prove the rationality theorem for normal pairs in the complex
analytic setting. The proof is essentially the same as the one for algebraic varieties
explained in [Fu3]. In Section 4.4, we deﬁne Kleiman–Mori cones for projective
morphisms of complex analytic spaces. Then we prove Kleiman’s ampleness crite-
rion in the complex analytic setting. In Section 4.5, we brieﬂy explain Nakayama’s
ﬁniteness without proof for the reader’s convenience. Note that in this book we do
not need it except in the proof of Corollary 1.1.8. Then, in Section 4.6, we prove
the cone theorem for normal pairs in the complex analytic setting. The results
in Section 4.6 are easy consequences of the basepoint-free theorem in Section 4.2
and the rationality theorem in Section 4.3. In the ﬁnal section: Section 4.7, we
prove Theorem 1.1.7 as an easy application of the vanishing theorem for projective
quasi-log schemes.

     Chapter 5: In Chapter 5, we treat some supplementary results. In Section
5.1, we discuss lengths of extremal rational curves. The result in Section 5.1 seems
to be indispensable for the minimal model program with scaling. Here, we use the
framework of quasi-log schemes. In Section 5.2, we discuss Shokurov’s polytopes
and some applications. The results in this section are well known and have already
played an important role in the usual algebraic setting. In Section 5.3, we prove
the basepoint-free theorem of log canonical pairs for R-Cartier divisors. It can
be seen as an application of the cone theorem. In Section 5.4, which is the ﬁnal
section of this chapter, we prove the main result of this book, that is, the cone and
contraction theorem of normal pairs for projective morphisms between complex
analytic spaces: Theorem 1.1.5.

     Chapter 6: Chapter 6 is devoted to some advanced topics. In Section 6.1, we
quickly review the theory of quasi-log complex analytic spaces without proof. The
reader can ﬁnd all the details in [Fu14]. In Section 6.2, we explain the basepoint-
free theorem of Reid–Fukuda type for log canonical pairs in the complex analytic
setting (see Theorem 6.2.1). The proof of Theorem 6.2.1 needs the framework of
quasi-log complex analytic spaces and is much harder than the one for the usual
basepoint-free theorem (see Theorem 4.2.1). In Section 6.3, we review the eﬀective
freeness and very ampleness for log canonical pairs in the complex analytic setting.
In Section 6.4, we explain some results on the minimal model program for projective
morphisms between complex analytic spaces established in [Fu11]. In Section 6.5,
we discuss the rational chain connectedness and its application to kawamata log
                             1.4. PRECISE CONTENTS                              13


terminal singularities. Here, we use some results obtained in [Fu11] and explained
in Section 6.4.
    Appendix: In this appendix, we correct some minor mistakes in [Fu5] for the
reader’s convenience.
                                    CHAPTER 2


                                Preliminaries

    In this chapter, we will collect basic deﬁnitions and results necessary for this
book. In Section 2.1, we will discuss singularities of pairs for complex analytic
spaces and explain various basic properties. In Section 2.2, we will treat relatively
ample and relatively nef R-line bundles in the complex analytic setting for the
reader’s convenience. In Section 2.3, we will introduce the notion of non-lc ideal
sheaves for normal complex varieties and prove some basic properties.

                            2.1. Singularities of pairs
    In this section, we will collect basic deﬁnitions and results necessary for this
book. For the details, see [Fu3], [Fu5], [Fu11], and so on. Since we are working in
the complex analytic setting, some of them become subtle.
    Let us start with the deﬁnition of singularities of pairs, which is indispensable
in the theory of minimal models.
     2.1.1 (Singularities of pairs, log canonical centers, and non-lc loci). We consider
a normal complex variety X. Let Xsm denote the smooth locus of X. Then the
canonical sheaf ωX of X is the unique reﬂexive sheaf whose restriction to Xsm is
isomorphic to the sheaf ΩnXsm , where n = dim X. Let ∆ be an R-divisor on X, that
is, ∆ is a locally ﬁnite R-linear combination of prime divisors on X. We say that
KX + ∆ is R-Cartier at x ∈ X if there exist an open neighborhood Ux of x and a
Weil divisor KUx on Ux with OUx (KUx ) ≃ ωX |Ux such that KUx +∆|Ux is R-Cartier,
that is, KUx + ∆|Ux is a ﬁnite R-linear combination of Cartier divisors on Ux . For
any subset L of X, we say that KX + ∆ is R-Cartier at L if it is R-Cartier at any
point x of L. We simply say that KX + ∆ is R-Cartier when KX + ∆ is R-Cartier
at any point x ∈ X. Unfortunately, however, we can not always deﬁne KX globally
with OX (KX ) ≃ ωX . In general, it only exists locally on X. We usually use the
symbol KX as a formal divisor class with an isomorphism OX (KX ) ≃ ωX and call
it the canonical divisor of X if there is no danger of confusion.
     Let f : Y → X be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a normal complex
variety Y . Suppose that KX + ∆ is R-Cartier in the above sense. We take a small
Stein open subset U of X where KU + ∆|U is a well-deﬁned R-Cartier R-divisor on
U . In this situation, we can deﬁne Kf −1 (U ) and KU such that f∗ Kf −1 (U ) = KU .
Then we can write
                            Kf −1 (U ) = f ∗ (KU + ∆|U ) + EU
as usual. Note that EU is a well-deﬁned R-divisor on f −1 (U ) such that f∗ EU = ∆|U .
Then we have the following formula
                                             X
                      KY = f ∗ (KX + ∆) +        a(E, X, ∆)E
                                                E

                                           15
16                                2. PRELIMINARIES

                                      P
as in the algebraic case. We note that E a(E, X, ∆)E is a globally well-deﬁned
R-divisor on Y such that
                                         !
                          X
                             a(E, X, ∆)E         = EU
                             E                  f −1 (U )

although KX and KY are well deﬁned only locally.
     If ∆ is a boundary R-divisor, that is, all the coeﬃcients of ∆ are in [0, 1]∩R, and
a(E, X, ∆) ≥ −1 holds for any f : Y → X and every f -exceptional divisor E, then
(X, ∆) is called a log canonical pair. If (X, ∆) is log canonical and a(E, X, ∆) > −1
for any f : Y → X and every f -exceptional divisor E, then (X, ∆) is called a purely
log terminal pair. If (X, ∆) is purely log terminal and ⌊∆⌋ = 0, that is, the
coeﬃcients of ∆ are in [0, 1) ∩ R, then (X, ∆) is called a kawamata log terminal
pair. When ∆ = 0 and a(E, X, 0) ≥ 0 (resp. > 0) for any f : Y → X and every
f -exceptional divisor E, we simply say that X has only canonical singularities
(resp. terminal singularities). In this book, we will only use log canonical pairs and
kawamata log terminal pairs.
     More generally, let X be a normal complex variety and let ∆ be an eﬀective
R-divisor on X. We say that (X, ∆) is log canonical (resp. kawamata log terminal)
at x ∈ X if there exists an open neighborhood Ux of x such that (Ux , ∆|Ux ) is a
log canonical pair (resp. kawamata log terminal pair). Let L be any subset of X.
We say that (X, ∆) is log canonical (resp. kawamata log terminal) at L if (X, ∆)
is log canonical (resp. kawamata log terminal) at any point x of L. We note that
(X, ∆) is log canonical (resp. kawamata log terminal) in the above sense if and only
if (X, ∆) is log canonical (resp. kawamata log terminal) at any point x of X.
     Let X be a normal complex variety and let ∆ be an eﬀective R-divisor on X
such that KX + ∆ is R-Cartier. The image of E with a(E, X, ∆) = −1 for some
f : Y → X such that (X, ∆) is log canonical around general points of f (E) is called
a log canonical center of (X, ∆). The non-lc locus of (X, ∆), denoted by Nlc(X, ∆),
is the smallest closed subset Z of X such that the complement (X \ Z, ∆|X\Z ) is log
canonical. We can deﬁne a natural complex analytic space structure on Nlc(X, ∆)
by the non-lc ideal sheaf JNLC (X, ∆) of (X, ∆). For the deﬁnition of JNLC (X, ∆),
see Section 2.3 below.
     The above deﬁnition is compatible with the usual deﬁnition for algebraic vari-
eties.
     Remark 2.1.2 (cf. [Ma, Proposition 4-4-4]). Let (X, ∆) be a pair consisting
of a normal algebraic variety X and an eﬀective R-divisor on X such that KX + ∆
is R-Cartier. Then (X, ∆) is kawamata log terminal (resp. log canonical) in the
usual sense (see [Fu3], [Fu5], and so on) if and only if (X an , ∆an ) is kawamata log
terminal (resp. log canonical) in the above sense, where X an is the complex analytic
space naturally associated to X and let ∆an be the R-divisor on X an associated to
∆.
     The following lemma is well known for algebraic varieties.
     Lemma 2.1.3. Let X be a normal complex variety and let ∆ be an eﬀective R-
divisor on X such that KX +∆ is R-Cartier. Let P be a point of X and let Di be an
                                                                                 
                                                                        Pk
eﬀective Cartier divisor on X with P ∈ Supp Di for every i. If X, ∆ + i=1 Di
is log canonical at P , then k ≤ dim X holds.
                             2.1. SINGULARITIES OF PAIRS                                       17


     We omit the proof of Lemma 2.1.3 here since the usual proof for algebraic
varieties can work without any changes (see, for example, [Fu3, Lemma 13.2]). We
will use Lemma 2.1.3 in order to create a new log canonical center.
    In this book, we sometimes implicitly use Serre’s GAGA.
    2.1.4 (Serre’s GAGA). Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism of complex
analytic spaces and let F be a ﬁber of π : X → Y . Then F is projective. Hence we
can apply various results of projective schemes to F with the aid of Serre’s GAGA
(see [Se]).
    In the theory of minimal models, we need the notion of R-line bundles and
Q-line bundles.
    2.1.5 (Line bundles, R-line bundles, and Q-line bundles). Let X be a complex
analytic space and let Pic(X) denote the group of line bundles on X, that is, the
Picard group of X. An element of Pic(X) ⊗Z R (resp. Pic(X) ⊗Z Q) is called an
R-line bundle (resp. a Q-line bundle) on X. In this book, we usually write the group
law of Pic(X) ⊗Z R additively for simplicity of notation. Hence we sometimes use
mL to denote L⊗m for L ∈ Pic(X) and m ∈ Z.
    We also need the notion of R-divisors and Q-divisors.
    2.1.6 (Divisors, R-divisors, and Q-divisors). Let X be a reduced equidimen-
sional complex analytic space. A prime divisor on X is an irreducible and reduced
closed analytic subspace of codimension one. An R-divisor D on X is a formal sum

emphasize the condition that ai ∈ Z for every i. If 0 ≤ ai ≤ 1 (resp. ai ≤ 1) holds

    Let D be an R-divisor on X and let x be a point of X. If D is written as a ﬁnite
R-linear (resp. Q-linear) combination of Cartier divisors on some open neighborhood
of x, then D is said to be R-Cartier at x (resp. Q-Cartier at x). If D is R-Cartier
(resp. Q-Cartier) at x for every x ∈ X, then D is said to be R-Cartier (resp. Q-
Cartier). More generally, for any subset L of X, if D is R-Cartier (resp. Q-Cartier)
at x for every x ∈ L, then D is said to be R-Cartier (resp. Q-Cartier) at L. Note
that a Q-Cartier R-divisor D is automatically a Q-Cartier Q-divisor by deﬁnition.
If D is a ﬁnite R-linear (resp. Q-linear) combination of Cartier divisors on X, then
we sometimes say that D is a globally R-Cartier R-divisor (resp. globally Q-Cartier
Q-divisor).
    Two R-divisors D1 and D2 are said to be linearly equivalent if D1 − D2 is a
principal Cartier divisor. The linear equivalence is denoted by D1 ∼ D2 . Two R-
divisors D1 and D2 are said to be R-linearly equivalent (resp. Q-linearly equivalent)
if D1 − D2 is a ﬁnite R-linear (resp. Q-linear) combination of principal Cartier
divisors. When D1 is R-linearly (resp. Q-linearly) equivalent to D2 , we write D1 ∼R
D2 (resp. D1 ∼Q D2 ).
    Example 2.1.7. Let X be a non-compact Riemann surfaceP      and let {Pk }∞
                                                                             k=1
                                                                 ∞
be a set of mutually distinct discrete points of X. We put D := k=1 k1 Pk . Then
D is obviously a Q-Cartier Q-divisor on X. However, D is not a ﬁnite Q-linear
combination of Cartier divisors on X.
    We note that in this book we can almost always assume that Supp D has only
ﬁnitely many irreducible components.
    2.1.8 (Hybrids of R-line bundles and R-Cartier divisors). In this book, we
usually treat hybrids of R-line bundles and R-Cartier divisors.
    Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism between complex analytic spaces and
let W be a compact subset of Y . Let A and B be R-Cartier divisors on X and let
L and M be R-line bundles on X.
    We sometimes say that
                                  L + A ∼R M + B
holds over some open neighborhood U of W . This means:
      (i) We implicitly assume that A|π−1 (U ) and B|π−1 (U ) are ﬁnite R-linear combi-
          nations of Cartier divisors on π −1 (U ). Thus we can obtain R-line bundles
          A and B naturally associated to A|π−1 (U ) and B|π−1 (U ) , respectively.
     (ii) In Pic(π −1 (U )) ⊗Z R, the following equality
                           L|π−1 (U ) + A = M|π−1 (U ) + B
         holds.
If X is a normal complex variety and U is a relatively compact open subset of
Y , then A|π−1 (U ) and B|π−1 (U ) are automatically ﬁnite R-linear combinations of
Cartier divisors on π −1 (U ). Therefore, (i) is harmless for applications.
     Similarly, we say that L + A is π-ample over some open neighborhood U of W
if A|π−1 (U ) is a ﬁnite R-linear combination of Cartier divisors on π −1 (U ), A is the
R-line bundle naturally associated to A|π−1 (U ) , and L|π−1 (U ) + A is π-ample over
U , that is, L|π−1 (U ) + A is a ﬁnite positive R-linear combination of π-ample line
bundles on π −1 (U ).
                              2.1. SINGULARITIES OF PAIRS                                19


     2.1.9. Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism of complex analytic spaces
such that X is a normal complex variety and let ∆ be an R-divisor on X such that
KX + ∆ is R-Cartier. Let y be an arbitrary point of Y and let Uy be any relatively
compact Stein open neighborhood of y ∈ Y . In this case, we can always ﬁnd a Weil
divisor Kπ−1 (Uy ) on π −1 (Uy ) such that Oπ−1 (Uy ) (Kπ−1 (Uy ) ) ≃ ωπ−1 (Uy ) holds since
π is projective and Uy is Stein. Since Uy is relatively compact, Supp ∆|π−1 (Uy ) has
only ﬁnitely many irreducible components. Thus, we can easily see that Kπ−1 (Uy ) +
∆|π−1 (Uy ) is a globally R-Cartier R-divisor on π −1 (Uy ). Moreover, for any R-line
bundle L on X, we can take a globally R-Cartier R-divisor L on π −1 (Uy ) such that
L|π−1 (Uy ) is the R-line bundle naturally associated to L.
     In the theory of minimal models, we often use the following formulation. We
will repeatedly use it in subsequent sections.
    2.1.10. Let X be a normal complex variety. A real vector space spanned by the
prime divisors on X is denoted by WDivR (X), which has a canonical basis given
by the prime divisors. Let D be an element of WDivR (X). Then the sup norm of
D with respect to this basis is denoted by ||D||. Note that an R-divisor D on X is
an element of WDivR (X) if and only if Supp D has only ﬁnitely many irreducible
components.
    Let V be a ﬁnite-dimensional aﬃne subspace of WDiv R (X), which is deﬁned
over the rationals. We put
                  R(V ; x) := {∆ ∈ V | KX + ∆ is R-Cartier at x}.
It is obvious that R(V ; x) is an aﬃne subspace of V . We take an arbitrary element
∆ of R(V ; x). Then KX + ∆ is R-Cartier at x by deﬁnition. Therefore, there exists
a small open neighborhood Ux of x such that
                                                  X

                  R(V ; L) := {∆ ∈ V | KX + ∆ is R-Cartier at L}.

                                              \

after shrinking X around L suitably, we can construct a projective bimeromorphic
morphism f : Y → X from a smooth complex analytic space Y such that Exc(f )
and Exc(f ) ∪ Supp f∗−1 Θ are simple normal crossing divisors on Y , where Exc(f )
denotes the exceptional locus of f : Y → X. Thus, for any ∆ ∈ R(V ; L), we can

such that Supp ∆Y is a simple normal crossing divisor on Y . In this situation,
(X, ∆) is log canonical at L if and only if ∆ is eﬀective at L and the coeﬃcients of
∆Y are less than or equal to one over L. Hence, we can easily check that
                    L(V ; L) := {∆ ∈ V | KX + ∆ is log canonical at L}
is a rational polytope contained in R(V ; L). We can also check that there exists an
open neighborhood U of L such that (U, ∆|U ) is log canonical for every ∆ ∈ L(V ; L).
    2.1.11. Let X be a complex analytic space. An analytic subset (resp. A locally
closed analytic subset) of X is the support of a closed analytic subspace (resp. a
locally closed analytic subspace) of X. A Zariski open subset of X means the
complement of an analytic subset. We note the following easy example.
   Example 2.1.12. We consider ∆ := {z ∈ C | |z| < 1} and ∆∗ := ∆ \ {0}. Then

   2.1.13. A subset S of a complex analytic space X is said to be analytically
meagre if                           [
                                S⊂      Yn ,
                                            n∈N
where each Yn is a locally closed analytic subset of X of codimension ≥ 1.
    Let X be a complex analytic space. We say that a property P holds for an an-
alytically suﬃciently general point x ∈ X when P holds for every point x contained
in X \ S for some analytically meagre subset S of X.
    Let π : X → Y be a morphism of analytic spaces. Similarly, we say that a
property P holds for an analytically suﬃciently general ﬁber of π : X → Y when P
holds for π −1 (y) for every y ∈ Y \ S, where S is some analytically meagre subset
of Y .
   In this book, we will freely use the following facts, which can be found in [BS,
Chapter III].
     2.1.14. Let π : X → Y be a projective surjective morphism of complex analytic
spaces and let L be a line bundle on X. If Rp π∗ L = 0 holds, then H p (F, L|F ) = 0
for an analytically suﬃciently general ﬁber F of π : X → Y . If H 0 (F, L|F ) ̸= 0 for
an analytically suﬃciently general ﬁber F of π : X → Y , then π∗ L ̸= 0 holds.
         We will use the following convention throughout this book.
     2.1.15. The expression ‘... for every m ≫ 0’ means that ‘there exists a positive
real number m0 such that ... for every m ≥ m0 .’
          2.2. RELATIVELY AMPLE AND RELATIVELY NEF R-LINE BUNDLES                   21


          2.2. Relatively ample and relatively nef R-line bundles
     In this section, we will collect some basic properties of relatively nef and rel-
atively ample R-line bundles for the reader’s convenience. We will frequently use
them in subsequent sections.
     Let us recall the deﬁnition of projective morphisms of complex analytic spaces
for the sake of completeness.
     Definition 2.2.1 (Projective morphisms of complex analytic spaces). Let
π : X → Y be a proper morphism of complex analytic spaces and let L be a line
bundle on X. Then L is said to be π-very ample or relatively very ample over Y if
L is π-free, that is,
                                   π ∗ π∗ L → L
is surjective, and the induced morphism
                                   X → PY (π∗ L)
over Y is a closed embedding. A line bundle L on X is called π-ample or ample
over Y if for any point y ∈ Y there are an open neighborhood U of y and a positive
integer m such that L⊗m |π−1 (U ) is relatively very ample over U . Let D be a Cartier
divisor on X. Then we say that D is π-very ample, π-free, and π-ample if the line
bundle OX (D) is so, respectively. We note that π : X → Y is said to be projective
when there exists a π-ample line bundle on X.
    For the basic properties of π-ample line bundles, see [BS, Chapter IV] and
[Na2, Chapter II. §1.c. Ample line bundles]. Since we are mainly interested in
R-line bundles in this book, the following easy lemma is indispensable.
     Lemma 2.2.2. Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism between complex ana-
lytic spaces and let W be a compact subset of Y . Let L be an R-line bundle on X.
Then the following two conditions are equivalent.
       (i) L is π-ample over W , that is, L|π−1 (w) is ample in the usual sense for
           every w ∈ W .
      (ii) L is π-ample over some open neighborhood U of W , that is, L|π−1 (U ) is a
           ﬁnite positive R-linear combination of π|π−1 (U ) -ample line bundles.
   Sketch of Proof of Lemma 2.2.2. It is obvious that (i) follows from (ii).
Hence it is suﬃcient to prove that (ii) follows from (i). It is an easy exercise to
modify the proof of [FM2, Lemmas 6.1 and 6.2] suitably with the aid of [Na1,
Proposition 1.4].                                                                
    Throughout this book, we will freely use Lemma 2.2.2 without mentioning it
explicitly. The following lemma is more or less well known to the experts. We
describe it here for the sake of completeness.
    Lemma 2.2.3. Let π : X → Y be a projective surjective morphism of complex
analytic spaces such that X and Y are both irreducible. Let L be a line bundle on
X. Assume that L|π−1 (y) is ample for some y ∈ Y . Then there exists a Zariski
open neighborhood U of y in Y and a positive integer m such that L⊗m |π−1 (U ) is
π-very ample over U . In particular, L|π−1 (U ) is π-ample over U .
   Proof. It is well known that there exists a small open neighborhood U1 of y in
Y such that L|π−1 (U1 ) is π-ample over U1 (see [Na1, Proposition 1.4]). Therefore,
22                              2. PRELIMINARIES


we can take some positive integer m such that L⊗m is π-very ample over some small
open neighborhood U2 of y in Y . We consider π ∗ π∗ L⊗m → L⊗m . It is obviously
surjective over U2 . Therefore,
                                                    
                    π Supp Coker(π ∗ π∗ L⊗m → L⊗m ) ∩ U2 = ∅.
Then we put
                                                           
                  U3 := Y \ π Supp Coker(π ∗ π∗ L⊗m → L⊗m ) .
Hence U3 is a non-empty Zariski open subset of Y such that y ∈ U3 and that
π ∗ π∗ L⊗m → L⊗m is surjective over U3 . We put
                                             

Then I is a coherent ideal sheaf on X. We L  take the blow-up p : Z → X of X along

                                                          

     As an application of Lemma 2.2.3, we have:
    Lemma 2.2.4. Let π : X → Y be a projective surjective morphism of complex
analytic spaces. Let L be an R-line bundle on X. Assume that L|π−1 (y) is ample
for some y ∈ Y . Then there exists a Zariski open neighborhood U of y in Y such
that L|π−1 (U ) is π-ample over U .
    In the theory of minimal models, we have to treat R-line bundles. Therefore,
Lemma 2.2.4 is indispensable. Since we can not directly apply geometric arguments
to R-line bundles, Lemma 2.2.4 is not so obvious.

We take an irreducible component Xj of X with j ∈ J1 . By applying Lemma 2.2.3

    By Lemma 2.2.4, we can easily obtain:
    Lemma 2.2.5. Let π : X → Y be a projective surjective morphism of complex
analytic spaces. Let L be an R-line bundle on X. Assume that L|π−1 (y0 ) is nef for
some y0 ∈ Y . Then there exists an analytically meagre subset S such that L|π−1 (y)
is nef for every y ∈ Y \ S.
    Although Lemma 2.2.5 is easy, it will play a very important role in our frame-
work of the minimal model program of complex analytic spaces. We note that we
can not make S a Zariski closed subset of Y in Lemma 2.2.5.
     Proof of Lemma 2.2.5. We take a π-ample line bundle H on X. Then (mL+
H)|π−1 (y0 ) is ample for every positive integer m. Therefore, by Lemma 2.2.4, for
each m ∈ Z>0 , we can take a Zariski openSneighborhood Um of y0 in Y such that
mL + H is π-ample over Um . We put S := m∈Z>0 (Y \ Um ). Then (mL + H)|π−1 (y)
is ample for every m ∈ Z>0 and every y ∈ Y \ S. This means that L|π−1 (y) is nef
for every y ∈ Y \ S.                                                            
     The following obvious corollary of Lemma 2.2.5 is also useful for geometric
applications. We note that we sometimes have to treat a countably inﬁnite set of
line bundles.
     Corollary 2.2.6. Let π : X → Y be a projective surjective morphism of com-
plex analytic spaces. Let Li be an R-line bundle on X for i ∈ N. Assume that
Li |π−1 (y0 ) is nef for some y0 ∈ Y and for every i ∈ N. Then there exists an ana-
lytically meagre subset S such that Li |π−1 (y) is nef for every y ∈ Y \ S and every
i ∈ N. Therefore, if H is any π-ample R-line bundle on X, then (H + Li )|π−1 (y) is
ample for every y ∈ Y \ S and every i ∈ N.
    Proof. By Lemma 2.2.5, for each i ∈ N, we can ﬁnd an analyticallySmeagre
subset Si of Y such that Li |π−1 (y) is nef for every y ∈ Y \ Si . We put S := i∈N Si .
Then it is easy to see that S is a desired analytically meagre subset of Y .        
    By the proof of Lemma 2.2.5 and Corollary 2.2.6, we have:
    Remark 2.2.7. In Lemma 2.2.5 and Corollary 2.2.6, we can make Y \ S a
countable intersection of non-empty Zariski open subsets of Y .

     In this book, we need the following Bertini-type theorem for JNLC (X, ∆).
     Lemma 2.3.3 ([Fu3, Proposition 7.5]). Let X be a normal complex variety and

holds outside the base locus Bs Λ of Λ for every element D of Λ \ S and every

(see [BM2, Theorem 13.2]), we can take a projective bimeromorphic morphism
f : Z → X from a smooth complex variety Z with KZ + ∆Z = f ∗ (KX + ∆) such
that Supp ∆Z is a simple normal crossing divisor on Z. By replacing X with
X \ Bs Λ, we may further assume that Bs Λ = ∅. By Bertini’s theorem, there exists
an analytically meagre subset S of Λ such that f ∗ D is smooth, f ∗ D = f∗−1 D,
f ∗ D and Supp ∆Z have no common irreducible components, and the support of
f ∗ D + Supp ∆Z is a simple normal crossing divisor on Z for every element D of
Λ\S. Then KZ +∆Z +f ∗ tD = f ∗ (KX +∆+tD) holds over X † with f ∗ tD = tf∗−1 D.

                                   CHAPTER 3


                          Vanishing theorems

     In this chapter, we will treat vanishing theorems. In Section 3.1, we will brieﬂy
review some vanishing theorems for analytic simple normal crossing pairs without
proof. Theorem 3.1.5 is one of the main ingredients of this book. The reader can
ﬁnd all the details in [Fu13] (see also [FF] and [Fu15]). In Section 3.2, we will
explain vanishing theorems of Reid–Fukuda type although we do not need them in
this book. Then, in Section 3.3, we will establish some useful vanishing theorems
for normal pairs by using the results explained in Section 3.1. As an application of
Section 3.3, we will prove basic properties of log canonical centers in Section 3.4.
They will play a crucial role in this book.

   3.1. Vanishing theorems for analytic simple normal crossing pairs
    In this section, let us quickly recall some vanishing theorems established in
[Fu13] (see also [FF] and [Fu15]). Let us start with the deﬁnition of analytic
simple normal crossing pairs.
    Definition 3.1.1 (Analytic simple normal crossing pairs). Let X be a simple
normal crossing divisor on a smooth complex analytic space M and let B be an R-
divisor on M such that Supp(B + X) is a simple normal crossing divisor on M and
that B and X have no common irreducible components. Then we put D := B|X
and consider the pair (X, D). We call (X, D) an analytic globally embedded simple
normal crossing pair and M the ambient space of (X, D).
    If the pair (X, D) is locally isomorphic to an analytic globally embedded simple
normal crossing pair at any point of X and the irreducible components of X and
D are all smooth, then (X, D) is called an analytic simple normal crossing pair.
    When (X, D) is an analytic simple normal crossing pair, X has an invertible
dualizing sheaf ωX since it is Gorenstein. We use the symbol KX as a formal divisor
class with an isomorphism OX (KX ) ≃ ωX if there is no danger of confusion. Note
that we can not always deﬁne KX globally with OX (KX ) ≃ ωX . In general, it only
exists locally on X.
    Remark 3.1.2. Let X be a smooth complex analytic space and let D be an
R-divisor on X such that Supp D is a simple normal crossing divisor on X. Then,
by considering M := X × C, we can see (X, D) as an analytic globally embedded
simple normal crossing pair.
    The notion of strata, which is a generalization of that of log canonical centers,
plays a crucial role.
    Definition 3.1.3 (Strata). Let (X, D) be an analytic simple normal crossing
pair such that D is eﬀective. Let ν : X ν → X be the normalization. We put
                             KX ν + Θ = ν ∗ (KX + D).
                                          27
28                            3. VANISHING THEOREMS


This means that Θ is the union of ν∗−1 D and the inverse image of the singular locus
of X. If S is an irreducible component of X or the ν-image of some log canonical
center of (X ν , Θ), then S is called a stratum of (X, D).
     We recall Siu’s theorem on coherent analytic sheaves, which is a special case of
[Si, Theorem 4].
   Theorem 3.1.4. Let F be a coherent sheaf on a complex analytic space X.
Then there exists a locally ﬁnite family {Yi }i∈I of complex analytic subvarieties of
X such that
                          AssOX,x (Fx ) = {px,1 , . . . , px,r(x) }
holds for every point x ∈ X, where px,1 , . . . , px,r(x) are the prime ideals of OX,x
associated to the irreducible components of the germs Yi,x of Yi at x with x ∈ Yi .
We note that each Yi is called an associated subvariety of F.
     Now we are ready to state the main result of [Fu13].
    Theorem 3.1.5 ([Fu13, Theorem 1.1]). Let (X, ∆) be an analytic simple nor-
mal crossing pair such that ∆ is a boundary R-divisor on X. Let f : X → Y be a
projective morphism to a complex analytic space Y and let L be a line bundle on X.
Let q be an arbitrary non-negative integer. Then we have the following properties.
      (i) (Strict support condition). If L − (ωX + ∆) is f -semiample, then every
          associated subvariety of Rq f∗ L is the f -image of some stratum of (X, ∆).
     (ii) (Vanishing theorem). If L − (ωX + ∆) ∼R f ∗ H holds for some π-ample
          R-line bundle H on Y , where π : Y → Z is a projective morphism to a
          complex analytic space Z, then we have
                                  R p π∗ R q f ∗ L = 0
          for every p > 0.
    We note that Theorem 3.1.5 is one of the main ingredients of this book. Or, we
can see this book as an application of Theorem 3.1.5. We make a supplementary
remark on Theorem 3.1.5.
     Remark 3.1.6. In Theorem 3.1.5 (and Theorem 3.2.3 below), we always as-
sume that ∆ is globally R-Cartier, that is, ∆ is a ﬁnite R-linear combination of
Cartier divisors. We note that if the support of ∆ has only ﬁnitely many irre-
ducible components then it is globally R-Cartier. Since we are mainly interested in
the standard setting explained in 1.1.3, this assumption is harmless to geometric
applications. Under this assumption, we can obtain an R-line bundle N on X nat-
urally associated to L − (ωX + ∆). The assumption in (i) means that N is a ﬁnite
positive R-linear combination of π-semiample line bundles on X. The assumption
in (ii) says that N = f ∗ H holds in Pic(X) ⊗Z R.
    In this book, we do not prove Theorem 3.1.5. A key result for the proof of
Theorem 3.1.5 is Takegoshi’s analytic generalization of Kollár’s torsion-free and
vanishing theorem (see [Ta]). For an alternative approach to Theorem 3.1.7, see
[Fu4, Corollaries 1.2 and 1.5].
    Theorem 3.1.7 (see [Ta]). Let f : X → Y be a projective surjective morphism
from a smooth irreducible complex analytic space X. Then Rq f∗ ωX is a torsion-free
coherent sheaf on Y for every q.
    3.1. VANISHING THEOREMS FOR ANALYTIC SIMPLE NORMAL CROSSING PAIRS             29


    Furthermore, let π : Y → Z be a projective morphism between complex analytic
spaces and let A be a π-ample line bundle on Y . Then Rp π∗ (A ⊗ Rq f∗ ωX ) = 0
holds for every p > 0 and every q.
    If Y is projective and Z is a point, then Theorem 3.1.7 is nothing but Kollár’s
famous torsion-free and vanishing theorem. Note that Takegoshi established much
more general results than Theorem 3.1.7 in [Ta] and the arguments in [Ta] are
analytic. An alternative approach to Theorem 3.1.7 in [Fu4] is also analytic. In
[Fu13], we proved the following generalization of Theorem 3.1.7 with the aid of
Saito’s theory of mixed Hodge modules (see [Sa1], [Sa2], [Sa3], [FFS], and [Sa4]).
Theorem 3.1.8 may help the reader understand Theorem 3.1.5.
    Theorem 3.1.8. Let (X, D) be an analytic simple normal crossing pair such
that D is reduced and let f : X → Y be a projective morphism of complex analytic
spaces. Then we have the following properties.
      (i) (Strict support condition). Every associated subvariety of Rq f∗ ωX (D) is
          the f -image of some stratum of (X, D) for every q.
     (ii) (Vanishing theorem). Let π : Y → Z be a projective morphism between
          complex analytic spaces and let A be a π-ample line bundle on Y . Then
                           Rp π∗ (A ⊗ Rq f∗ ωX (D)) = 0
         holds for every p > 0 and every q.
    From now on, let us brieﬂy explain how to prove Theorem 3.1.8 from Theorem
3.1.7 with the aid of Saito’s theory of mixed Hodge modules. In order to explain
the idea of the proof of Theorem 3.1.8, we need the following description of strata.
    3.1.9. Let (X, D) be an analytic simple normal crossing pair such that D is
reduced. For any positive integer k, we put
                                                       ∼
                         X [k] := {x ∈ X| multx X ≥ k} ,
where Z ∼ denotes the normalization of Z. Then X [k] is the disjoint union of the
intersections of k irreducible components of X, and is smooth. We have a reduced
simple normal crossing divisor D[k] ⊂ X [k] deﬁned by the pull-back of D by the
natural morphism X [k] → X. For any non-negative integer l, we put
                                 n                         o∼
                        D[k,l] := x ∈ X [k] multx D[k] ≥ l    .

We note that D[k,0] = X [k] holds by deﬁnition. We also note that dim D[k,l] =
n + 1 − k − l, where n = dim X. In this situation, S is a stratum of (X, D) if and
only if S is the image of an irreducible component of D[k,l] for some k > 0 and
l ≥ 0.
    As an application of Saito’s theory of mixed Hodge modules, we established
the following theorem in [FFS].
     Theorem 3.1.10 ([FFS, Corollary 1 and 4.7. Remark]). Let (X, D) be an
analytic simple normal crossing pair with dim X = n such that D is reduced and let
f : X → Y be a projective morphism to a smooth complex analytic space Y . Then
there is the weight spectral sequence
                  −q,i+q
                                M
               F E1      =            Ri f∗ ωD[k,l] /Y ⇒ Ri f∗ ωX/Y (D),
                          k+l=n+q+1
30                             3. VANISHING THEOREMS


degenerating at E2 , and its E1 -diﬀerential d1 splits so that the F E2−q,i+q are direct
factors of F E1−q,i+q .
    Now we can easily check Theorem 3.1.8 by using Theorems 3.1.7 and 3.1.10.
Here we only explain the idea of the proof of Theorem 3.1.8. For the details of the
proof, see [Fu13].
     Sketch of Proof of Theorem 3.1.8. First we prove (i). We may assume
that Y is a closed analytic subspace of a polydisc since the problem is local. There-
fore, it is suﬃcient to prove (i) under the extra assumption that Y itself is a poly-
L i In this case, ωY ≃ OY . By Theorem 3.1.7 and the description in 3.1.9,
disc.
   R f∗ ωD[k,l] satisﬁes the strict support condition. Hence, by using the spectral
sequence in Theorem 3.1.10, we obtain (i). Next, we treat (ii). We may assume that
Z is a polydisc and that Y is a closed analytic
                                                   subspace of Z × Pn . By Theorem
3.1.7, we see that R π∗ A ⊗ R f∗ ωD[k,l] = 0 holds for every p > 0. By applying
                      p           i

Theorem 3.1.10 to f : X → Y ,→ Z × Pn , we obtain the following spectral sequence:
                                  M
                   E1−q,i+q =            Ri f∗ ωD[k,l] ⇒ Ri f∗ ωX (D),
                             k+l=n+q+1

which degenerates at E2 such that its E1 -diﬀerential d1 splits. Hence, we can easily
check that (ii) holds true.                                                        
    The reader can ﬁnd an alternative approach to Theorem 3.1.8 without using
Saito’s theory of mixed Hodge modules in [FF]. Once we know Theorem 3.1.8, it
is not diﬃcult to prove Theorem 3.1.5. For the details, see [Fu13].

               3.2. Vanishing theorems of Reid–Fukuda type
     Although we do not need vanishing theorems of Reid–Fukuda type in this book,
we will shortly discuss them here for future usage. Let us start with the deﬁnition
of big R-line bundles for the reader’s convenience.
    Definition 3.2.1 (Big R-line bundles). Let π : X → Y be a projective mor-
phism of complex analytic spaces such that X is irreducible and let L be an R-line
bundle on X. If L is a ﬁnite positive R-linear combination of π-big line bundles on
X, then L is said to be big over Y or π-big over Y .
     We need the notion of nef and log big R-line bundles.
    Definition 3.2.2 (Nef and log big R-line bundles). Let (X, ∆) be an analytic
simple normal crossing pair such that ∆ is a boundary R-divisor on X, let f : X →
Y and π : Y → Z be projective morphisms between complex analytic spaces, and
let H be an R-line bundle on Y . Then H is said to be nef and log big over Z with
respect to f : (X, ∆) → Y if H · C ≥ 0 holds for every projective integral curve C on
Y such that π(C) is a point and H|f (S) can be written as a ﬁnite positive R-linear
combination of π-big line bundles on f (S) for every stratum S of (X, ∆).
     We note that if H is π-ample in Deﬁnition 3.2.2 then it is obviously nef and log
big over Z with respect to f : (X, ∆) → Y . Hence the following vanishing theorem
is a generalization of Theorem 3.1.5 (ii).
     Theorem 3.2.3 (Vanishing theorem of Reid–Fukuda type, see [Fu13, Theorem
1.2]). Let (X, ∆) be an analytic simple normal crossing pair such that ∆ is a bound-
ary R-divisor on X. Let f : X → Y and π : Y → Z be projective morphisms between
                    3.3. VANISHING THEOREMS FOR NORMAL PAIRS                         31


complex analytic spaces and let L be a line bundle on X. If L − (ωX + ∆) ∼R f ∗ H
holds such that H is an R-line bundle, which is nef and log big over Z with respect
to f : (X, ∆) → Y , on Y , then
                                   R p π∗ R q f ∗ L = 0
holds for every p > 0 and every q.
    The reader can ﬁnd the detailed proof of Theorem 3.2.3 in [Fu13], which is
harder than that of Theorem 3.1.5 (ii). As an easy application of Theorem 3.2.3,
we can establish the vanishing theorem of Reid–Fukuda type for log canonical pairs
in the complex analytic setting.
    Theorem 3.2.4 (Vanishing theorem of Reid–Fukuda type for log canonical
pairs). Let (X, ∆) be a log canonical pair and let π : X → Y be a projective mor-
phism of complex analytic spaces. Let L be a Q-Cartier integral Weil divisor on X.
Assume that L − (KX + ∆) is nef and big over Y and that (L − (KX + ∆))|C is big
over π(C) for every log canonical center C of (X, ∆). Then
                                   Rq π∗ OX (L) = 0
holds for every q > 0.
      Proof. The proof of [Fu5, Theorem 5.7.6] works by Theorem 3.2.3.               
      We leave the details of Theorems 3.2.3 and 3.2.4 for the interested readers.

                   3.3. Vanishing theorems for normal pairs
    In this section, we will prove some vanishing theorems, which are suitable
for geometric applications. Theorem 3.3.1 will play a crucial role in subsequent
sections. We note that the results in this section follow from Theorem 3.1.5.
     Theorem 3.3.1 (see [Fu3, Theorem 8.1]). Let π : X → Y be a projective mor-
phism of complex analytic spaces such that X is a normal complex variety and let
W be a compact subset of Y . Let ∆ be an eﬀective R-divisor on X such that KX +∆
is R-Cartier and let L be a line bundle on X. We assume that L − (KX + ∆) is
π-ample over W , that is, (L − (KX + ∆)) |π−1 (w) is ample for every w ∈ W  S . Let
{Ci }i∈I be any set of log canonical centers of the pair (X, ∆). We put V := i∈I Ci
with the reduced structure. We further assume that V is disjoint from the non-lc
locus Nlc(X, ∆) of (X, ∆). Then there exists some open neighborhood U of W such
that
                                  Ri π∗ (J ⊗ L) = 0
holds on U for every i > 0, where J := IV · JNLC (X, ∆) ⊂ OX and IV is the
deﬁning ideal sheaf of V on X. Therefore, the restriction map
                           π∗ L → π∗ (L|V ) ⊕ π∗ (L|Nlc(X,∆) )
is surjective on U and
                                 Ri π∗ (L|V ) = 0
holds on U for every i > 0. In particular, the restriction maps
                                    π∗ L → π∗ (L|V )
and
                                π∗ L → π∗ (L|Nlc(X,∆) )
are surjective on U .
32                              3. VANISHING THEOREMS


   The result and argument in Step 1 in the proof of Theorem 3.3.1 is the most
important part of this book. We will use them repeatedly in subsequent sections.
     Proof of Theorem 3.3.1. In Steps 1 and 2, we will use the strict support
condition (see Theorem 3.1.5 (i)) and the vanishing theorem (see Theorem 3.1.5
(ii)), respectively. The assumption that L − (KX + ∆) is π-ample over W will be
used only in Step 2.
     We take an arbitrary point w ∈ W . Then it is suﬃcient to prove the desired
vanishing theorem over some open neighborhood of w by the compactness of W .
Therefore, we may replace Y with a relatively compact Stein open neighborhood
of w and may assume that L − (KX + ∆) is π-ample over Y .
     Step 1. We can take a resolution of singularities f : Z → X of X such that f
is projective and that Supp f∗−1 ∆ ∪ Exc(f ) is a simple normal crossing divisor on
Z. We may further assme that f −1 (V ) is a simple normal crossing divisor on Z.
Then we can write

    The following remark is obvious by the proof of Theorem 3.3.1.
