   Theorem 5.3.1 will play an important role in the study of minimal models of
complex analytic spaces.

                  5.4. Proof of Main theorem: Theorem 1.1.5
   In this section, we will prove Theorem 1.1.5, which is the main theorem of this
book.
    Proof of Theorem 1.1.5. By Theorem 4.6.2 (1) and (2), we obtain the fol-
lowing equality
                                                                  X
    NE(X/Y ; W ) = NE(X/Y ; W )(KX +∆)≥0 + NE(X/Y ; W )Nlc(X,∆) +   Rj
satisfying (1), (2), and (3) in Theorem 1.1.5. By Theorem 4.6.2 (3), F in Theorem
1.1.5 (4) is rational and hence contractible at Nlc(X, ∆). Thus, by the contraction
theorem (see Theorem 4.6.1), we obtain the desired contraction morphism ϕF : X →
Z over Y after shrinking Y around W suitably. By Theorem 5.1.2, we see that (5)
holds. We note that (6) is nothing but Theorem 5.2.4. Finally, we will prove (7).
We may assume that KX +∆ is not π-nef over W . Then we can take a small positive
real number ε such that KX + ∆ + εH is not π-nef over W . By the cone theorem
(see Theorem 4.6.2 (2)), there exist only ﬁnitely many (KX + ∆ + εH)-negative
extremal rays R1 , . . . , Rk of NE(X/Y ; W ). We put
                                       −(KX + ∆) · Ri
                                 µi :=
                                           H · Ri
for every i. Then it is obvious that λ = max1≤i≤k µi . If λ = µi0 holds for 1 ≤ i0 ≤ k,
then (KX + ∆ + λH) · Ri0 = 0. By construction, KX + ∆ + λH is π-nef over W .
We ﬁnish the proof of Theorem 1.1.5.                                                 
                                  CHAPTER 6


                            Advanced topics

     In this ﬁnal chapter, we will discuss some advanced topics. In Section 6.1, we
will quickly review the theory of quasi-log complex analytic spaces without proof.
The reader can ﬁnd all the details in [Fu14]. In Section 6.2, we will explain the
basepoint-free theorem of Reid–Fukuda type for log canonical pairs in the complex
analytic setting (see Theorem 6.2.1). The proof of Theorem 6.2.1 needs the frame-
work of quasi-log complex analytic spaces and is much harder than the one for the
usual basepoint-free theorem (see Theorem 4.2.1). In Section 6.3, we will review the
eﬀective freeness and very ampleness for log canonical pairs in the complex analytic
setting. In Section 6.4, we will explain some results on the minimal model program
for projective morphisms between complex analytic spaces established in [Fu11].
In Section 6.5, we will discuss the rational chain connectedness and its application
to kawamata log terminal singularities.

                         6.1. On quasi-log structures
    In this section, we will brieﬂy explain the theory of quasi-log complex analytic
spaces without proof. In [Fu14], we will discuss quasi-log structures for complex
analytic spaces in detail. For the details of the theory of quasi-log schemes, see
[Fu5, Chapter 6]. Let us start with the deﬁnition of quasi-log complex analytic
spaces.
    Definition 6.1.1 (Quasi-log complex analytic spaces). A quasi-log complex
analytic space
                                                   
                            X, ω, f : (Z, BZ ) → X
is a complex analytic space X endowed with an R-line bundle (or a globally R-
Cartier divisor) ω on X, a closed analytic subspace X−∞ ⊊ X, and a ﬁnite collection
{C} of reduced and irreducible closed analytic subspaces of X such that there exists
a projective morphism f : (Z, BZ ) → X from an analytic globally embedded simple
normal crossing pair (Z, BZ ) satisfying the following properties:
     (1) f ∗ ω ∼R KZ + BZ .
     (2) The natural map OX → f∗ OZ (⌈−(BZ<1 )⌉) induces an isomorphism
                              ≃
                      IX−∞ −→ f∗ OZ (⌈−(BZ<1 )⌉ − ⌊BZ>1 ⌋),
         where IX−∞ is the deﬁning ideal sheaf of X−∞ on X.
     (3) The collection of closed analytic subvarieties {C} coincides with the f -
         images of (Z, BZ )-strata that are not included in X−∞ .
We often simply write [X, ω] to denote the above data
                                                     
                              X, ω, f : (Z, BZ ) → X
                                         69
70                               6. ADVANCED TOPICS


if there is no risk of confusion. The closed analytic subvarieties C are called the
qlc strata of [X, ω]. If a qlc stratum C is not an irreducible component of X,
then it is called a qlc center of [X, ω]. The closed analytic subspace X−∞ is
called the non-qlc locus of [X, ω]. We note that we sometimes use Nqlc(X, ω)
or Nqlc (X, ω, f : (Z, BZ ) → X) to denote X−∞ .
     Furthermore, if X−∞ = ∅ in the above deﬁnition, then
                                (X, ω, f : (Z, BZ ) → X)
is called a quasi-log canonical pair.
   For the details of Deﬁnition 6.1.1, see [Fu14, Deﬁnition 4.1]. The following
example is the most important one.
    Example 6.1.2 (Normal pairs). Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism of
complex analytic spaces such that X is a normal complex variety and let ∆ be an
eﬀective R-divisor on X such that KX + ∆ is R-Cartier. We usually call (X, ∆) a
normal pair. We replace Y with any relatively compact open subset of Y . Then
we can construct a projective bimeromorphic morphism f : Z → X with
                              KZ + BZ := f ∗ (KX + ∆)
such that Z is smooth and Supp BZ is a simple normal crossing divisor on Y . Then
                              f ∗ (KX + ∆) ∼R KZ + BZ
obviously holds and
                      JNLC (X, ∆) = f∗ OZ (⌈−(BZ<1 )⌉ − ⌊BZ>1 ⌋)
is a well-deﬁned coherent ideal sheaf on X which deﬁnes the non-lc locus Nlc(X, ∆)
of (X, ∆) (see Deﬁnition 2.3.1). By deﬁnition, C is a log canonical center of (X, ∆)
if and only if C is not contained in Nlc(X, ∆) and is the f -image of some log
canonical center of (Z, BZ=1 ). Hence,
                            (X, KX + ∆, f : (Z, BZ ) → X)
with X−∞ := Nlc(X, ∆) satisﬁes the conditions in Deﬁnition 6.1.1, that is,
                            (X, KX + ∆, f : (Z, BZ ) → X)
is a quasi-log complex analytic space. By construction, X−∞ = ∅ if and only if
(X, ∆) is log canonical.
    By Example 6.1.2, we can use the theory of quasi-log complex analytic spaces
to study normal pairs. A key result of the theory of quasi-log complex analytic
spaces is adjunction.
      Theorem 6.1.3 (Adjunction formula for quasi-log complex analytic spaces).
Let                                                            
                               X, ω, f : (Z, BZ ) → X
be a quasi-log complex analytic space and let X ′ be the union of X−∞ with a union
of some qlc strata of [X, ω]. Then, after replacing X with any relatively compact
open subset of X, we can construct a projective morphism f ′ : (Z ′ , BZ ′ ) → X ′ from
an analytic globally embedded simple normal crossing pair (Z ′ , BZ ′ ) such that
                                                                   
                             X ′ , ω ′ , f ′ : (Z ′ , BZ ′ ) → X ′
is a quasi-log complex analytic space with ω ′ = ω|X ′ and X−∞   ′
                                                                     = X−∞ . Moreover,
the qlc strata of [X , ω ] are exactly the qlc strata of [X, ω] that are included in X ′ .
                    ′   ′
               6.2. BASEPOINT-FREE THEOREM OF REID–FUKUDA TYPE                        71


   By Theorem 6.1.3, we can use inductive arguments for the study of quasi-log
complex analytic spaces. Note that theorem 6.1.3 follows from Theorem 3.1.5 (i).
By using Theorem 3.2.3, we can obtain the following vanishing theorems.
    Theorem 6.1.4 (Vanishing theorem I). Let
                                                         
                                X, ω, f : (Z, BZ ) → X
be a quasi-log complex analytic space and let π : X → Y be a projective morphism
between complex analytic spaces. Let L be a line bundle on X such that L − ω is nef
and log big over Y with respect to [X, ω], that is, L − ω is nef over Y and (L − ω)|C
is big over π(C) for every qlc stratum C of [X, ω]. Then
                                Ri π∗ (IX−∞ ⊗ L) = 0
holds for every i > 0. In particular, if X−∞ = ∅, then
                                      R i π∗ L = 0
holds for every i > 0.
    Theorem 6.1.5 (Vanishing theorem II). Let
                                                         
                                X, ω, f : (Z, BZ ) → X
be a quasi-log complex analytic space and let X ′ be the union of X−∞ with a union
of some qlc strata of [X, ω]. Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism between
complex analytic spaces and let L be a line bundle on X such that L − ω is nef over
Y and (L − ω)|C is big over π(C) for every qlc stratum C of [X, ω] which is not
contained in X ′ . Then
                                  Ri π∗ (IX ′ ⊗ L) = 0
holds for every i > 0, where IX ′ is the deﬁning ideal sheaf of X ′ on X. In particular,
if L − ω is ample over Y , then
                                 Ri π∗ (IX ′ ⊗ L) = 0
holds for every i > 0.
    We can see Theorem 6.1.5 as a generalization of the Kawamata–Viehweg–Nadel
vanishing theorem. For the details of the above theorems, see [Fu14, Section 4]. We
note that Theorems 6.1.4 and 6.1.5 generalize the results in Section 3.3 by Example
6.1.2.

             6.2. Basepoint-free theorem of Reid–Fukuda type
    The following theorem is a special case of [Fu14, Theorem 7.1], where we
formulate the basepoint-free theorem of Reid–Fukuda type for quasi-log complex
analytic spaces.
    Theorem 6.2.1 (Basepoint-free theorem of Reid–Fukuda type). Let π : X → Y
be a projective morphism of complex analytic space such that X is a normal complex
variety and let ∆ be an eﬀective R-divisor on X such that KX + ∆ is R-Cartier.
Let L be a π-nef line bundle on X such that aL − (KX + ∆) is nef and log big
over Y with respect to (X, ∆) for some positive real number a. This means that
aL − (KX + ∆) is nef and big over Y and that (aL − (KX + ∆))|C is big over
π(C) for every log canonical center C of (X, ∆). We assume that L⊗m |Nlc(X,∆) is
π-generated for every m ≫ 0. Then, after replacing Y with any relatively compact
open subset of Y , L⊗m is π-generated for every m ≫ 0.
72                             6. ADVANCED TOPICS


    Theorem 6.2.1 obviously generalizes the basepoint-free theorem: Theorem 4.2.1.
To the best knowledge of the author, there is no proof of Theorem 6.2.1 without
using the theory of quasi-log complex analytic spaces. Hence Theorem 6.2.1 is much
harder to prove than Theorem 4.2.1. For the details of Theorem 6.2.1, see [Fu14,
Section 7].

                 6.3. Eﬀective freeness and very ampleness
    In this section, we will brieﬂy explain the eﬀective freeness and the eﬀective
very ampleness for log canonical pairs in the complex analytic setting without proof.
The following theorem is a very special case of [Fu14, Theorem 8.1] by Example
6.1.2.
    Theorem 6.3.1 (Eﬀective freeness). Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism
between complex analytic spaces and let (X, ∆) be a log canonical pair. Let L be
a π-nef line bundle on X such that aL − (KX + ∆) is π-ample over Y for some
non-negative integer a. Then there exists a positive integer m = m(dim X, a), which
only depends on dim X and a, such that L⊗m is π-generated. Moreover, there exists
a positive integer m0 = m0 (dim X, a) depending only on dim X and a such that L⊗l
is π-generated for every l ≥ m0 .
     If KX + ∆ is Q-Cartier in Theorem 6.3.1, then we have:
    Theorem 6.3.2. In Theorem 6.3.1, if KX + ∆ is Q-Cartier, then we may
replace the assumption that aL − (KX + ∆) is π-ample over Y with a weaker one
that aL − (KX + ∆) is nef and log big over Y with respect to (X, ∆), that is,
aL − (KX + ∆) is nef and big over Y and (aL − (KX + ∆)) |C is big over π(C) for
every log canonical center C of (X, ∆).
   For the details of Theorem 6.3.2, see [Fu14, Theorem 8.2]. If L is π-ample in
Theorem 6.3.1, then we have the following eﬀective very ampleness.
    Theorem 6.3.3 (Eﬀective very ampleness). Let π : X → Y be a projective
morphism between complex analytic spaces and let (X, ∆) be a log canonical pair.
Let L be a π-ample line bundle on X such that aL − (KX + ∆) is π-nef over Y for
some non-negative integer a. Then there exists a positive integer m′ = m′ (dim X, a)
                                                ′
depending only on dim X and a such that L⊗m is π-very ample. Moreover, there
                           ′    ′
exists a positive integer m0 = m0 (dim X, a) depending only on dim X and a such
         ′
that L⊗l is π-very ample for every l′ ≥ m′0 .
    As above, Theorem 6.3.3 is a special case of [Fu14, Theorem 8.3] by Example
6.1.2. For the details see [Fu14, Section 8], where everything is formulated for
quasi-log complex analytic spaces.

                         6.4. Minimal model program
     In this section, we will shortly discuss some results established in [Fu11].
Roughly speaking, in [Fu11], we showed that [BCHM] and [HM2] can work
for projective morphisms between complex analytic spaces. Hence we have estab-
lished the ﬁnite generation for kawamata log terminal pairs in the complex analytic
setting.
                     6.5. ON RATIONAL CHAIN CONNECTEDNESS                          73


     Theorem 6.4.1 (Finite generation). Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism
of complex analytic spaces and let ∆ be an eﬀective Q-divisor on X such that (X, ∆)
is kawamata log terminal. Then
                                        M
                 R(X/Y, KX + ∆) :=          π∗ OX (⌊m(KX + ∆)⌋)
                                        m∈N

is a locally ﬁnitely generated graded OY -algebra.
    As a special case of Theorem 6.4.1, we have the following ﬁnite generation of
relative canonical rings.
    Corollary 6.4.2. Let π : X → Y be a projective morphism of complex analytic
spaces such that X is smooth and irreducible. Then the relative canonical ring
                                         M
                                                   ⊗m
                            R(X/Y ) :=        π∗ ω X
                                           m∈N

is a locally ﬁnitely generated graded OY -algebra.
    In the complex analytic setting, we established the minimal model program
with scaling as follows.
     Theorem 6.4.3 (Minimal model program with scaling for projective morphisms
of complex analytic spaces, see [Fu11, Theorem 1.7]). Let π : X → Y be a projective
surjective morphism of complex analytic spaces and let W be a compact subset of
Y . Assume that Y is Stein and that W is a Stein compact subset of Y such that
Γ(W, OY ) is noetherian. Let (X, ∆) be a kawamata log terminal pair such that ∆
is π-big and that X is Q-factorial over W . If C is an eﬀective R-divisor on X such
that KX + ∆ + C is kawamata log terminal and it is nef over W . Then we can
run the (KX + ∆)-minimal model program with scaling of C over Y around W .
More precisely, we have a ﬁnite sequence of ﬂips and divisorial contractions over
Y starting from (X, ∆):
                                  φ0             φ1     φm−1
             (X, ∆) =: (X0 , ∆0 ) 99K (X1 , ∆1 ) 99K · · · 99K (Xm , ∆m ),
where ∆i+1 := (ϕi )∗ ∆i for every i ≥ 0, such that (Xm , ∆m ) is a log terminal model
(resp. has a Mori ﬁber space structure) over some open neighborhood of W when
KX + ∆ is π-pseudo-eﬀective (resp. not π-pseudo-eﬀective). We note that each step
ϕi exists only after shrinking Y around W suitably. Hence we have to replace Y
with a small Stein open neighborhood of W repeatedly in the above process.
   For the details of Theorem 6.4.3, see [Fu11]. In Section 6.5, we will use Theo-
rem 6.4.3 in the case where W is a point.

                    6.5. On rational chain connectedness
     The results in this section seem to be more or less well known to the experts
although they are formulated and stated only for algebraic varieties in [HM1].
Here, we do not repeat the proof of [HM1] in the complex analytic setting. We
will use a diﬀerent approach.
    Definition 6.5.1 (Rational chain connectedness). Let X be a projective com-
plex analytic space. We say that X is rationally chain connected if for arbitrary
points P1 , P2 ∈ X there exists a connected curve C on X such that P1 , P2 ∈ C and
that every irreducible component of C is rational.
74                               6. ADVANCED TOPICS


     In Deﬁnition 6.5.1, X may be reducible and highly singular.
     Theorem 6.5.2. Let π : X → S be a projective morphism of complex analytic
spaces with π∗ OX ≃ OS such that (X, ∆) is log canonical. Assume that −(KX +∆)
is π-ample over some open neighborhood of P ∈ S. Then π −1 (P ) is rationally chain
connected.
    Proof. After shrinking S around P , we can naturally see [X, KX + ∆] as a
quasi-log complex analytic space with Nqlc(X, KX +∆) = ∅ (see Example 6.1.2 and
[Fu14]). Therefore, by [Fu14, Theorem 9.8], we obtain that π −1 (P ) is rationally
chain connected.                                                                
    Note that the proof of [Fu14, Theorem 9.8] essentially depends on [HM1].
Hence, it does not give an alternative proof of the results in [HM1] established for
algebraic varieties.
     Corollary 6.5.3. Let π : X → S be a projective bimeromorphic morphism
of normal complex varieties with π∗ OX ≃ OS such that (X, ∆) is kawamata log
terminal. Let P ∈ S be an arbitrary point. Assume that KX + ∆ is π-numerically
trivial over P , that is, (KX + ∆) · C = 0 holds for every curve C with π(C) = P .
Then π −1 (P ) is rationally chain connected.
     Proof. After shrinking S around P , we can ﬁnd an eﬀective Q-Cartier Q-
divisor D on X such that (X, ∆ + D) is still kawamata log terminal and that −D
is π-ample. Hence −(KX + ∆ + D) is π-ample over some open neighborhood of P .
Therefore, by Theorem 6.5.2, π −1 (P ) is rationally chain connected.        
     The following lemma is obvious. We will use it in the proof of Theorem 6.5.5.
     Lemma 6.5.4. Let g : Z → Y and f : Y → X be proper surjective morphisms of
complex analytic spaces. If (f ◦ g)−1 (P ) is rationally chain connected, then f −1 (P )
is also rationally chain connected.
     Proof. This is because (f ◦ g)−1 (P ) → f −1 (P ) is surjective.                 
    By using the minimal model program for projective morphisms between com-
plex analytic spaces (see [Fu11] and Theorem 6.4.3), we can prove the following
result as an easy application of Corollary 6.5.3.
     Theorem 6.5.5 (Kawamata log terminal singularities). Let X be a normal
complex variety such that (X, ∆) is kawamata log terminal for some eﬀective R-
divisor ∆ on X. Let f : Y → X be any proper bimeromorphic morphism from a
complex variety Y . Then f −1 (P ) is rationally chain connected for every P ∈ X.
     The author learned the following proof in [DH].
    Proof. Throughout this proof, we will freely shrink X around P without
mentioning it explicitly. By applying Chow’s lemma for proper bimeromorphic
morphisms (see [Hi, Corollary 2]) and taking a suitable resolution of singularities
(see [BM2]), we may assume that Y is smooth and f is projective by Lemma 6.5.4.
We may further assume that the exceptional locus Exc(f ) of f is a divisor and that
the union of the support of f∗−1 ∆ and Exc(f ) is a simple normal crossing divisor
on Y . Then we can write
                           KY + ∆Y = f ∗ (KX + ∆) + E
                       6.5. ON RATIONAL CHAIN CONNECTEDNESS                                 75


such that (Y, ∆Y ) is kawamata log terminal and that E is eﬀective with Supp E =
Exc(f ). By [Fu11] (see also Theorem 6.4.3), we can run a minimal model program
with respect to KY + ∆Y over X around P starting from (Y, ∆Y ):
                          φ0             φ1      φi−1             φi      φm−1
 (Y, ∆Y ) =: (Y0 , ∆Y0 ) 99K (Y1 , ∆Y1 ) 99K · · · 99K (Yi , ∆Yi ) 99K · · · 99K (Ym , ∆Ym ),
where ∆Yi+1 := (ϕi )∗ ∆Yi for every i ≥ 0, such that KYm + ∆Ym is semi-ample
over some open neighborhood of P . We note that each step ϕi exists only after
shrinking X around P suitably. We also note that f is a projective bimeromorphic
morphism. Hence KY + ∆Y is automatically big over X. Therefore, we ﬁnally get
a small projective bimeromorphic morphism fm : Ym → X such that KYm + ∆Ym =
  ∗                                      −1
fm  (KX + ∆) holds. By Corollary 6.5.3, fm  (P ) is rationally chain connected. By
applying Theorem 6.5.2 to each ﬂipping contraction and each divisorial contraction
in the above minimal model program, we can check that π −1 (P ) is rationally chain
connected with the aid of Lemma 6.5.4.                                           
     The following corollary of Theorem 6.5.5 is well known for proper rational maps
of algebraic varieties.
    Corollary 6.5.6. Let f : X 99K Y be a meromorphic map of complex analytic
spaces such that (X, ∆) is kawamata log terminal. Assume that there are no rational
curves on Y . Then f is a morphism.
    Proof. Let Γ be the graph of f : X 99K Y . By Theorem 6.5.5, any positive-
dimensional ﬁber of p : Γ → X is rationally chain connected, where p : Γ → X is
the projection. Since Y has no rational curves, p : Γ → X is an isomorphism. This
means that f is a morphism.                                                    
                             Erratum to [Fu5]

    Here, we will correct some small mistakes in [Fu5] for the reader’s convenience.
Let us correct some mathematical mistakes.
       • The proof of [Fu5, Lemma 2.4.5] has a small trouble. It is not clear
         whether the pull-back of E on a resolution of X is still in the movable
         cone or not. Hence it may be better to add the assumption that X is Q-
         factorial in [Fu5, Lemma 2.4.5]. Then, the proof of [Fu5, Lemma 2.4.5]
         works without replacing X with a resolution. Note that [Fu5, Lemma
         2.4.5] is used in the proof of [Fu5, Theorem 4.4.2] and that Z in the proof
         of [Fu5, Theorem 4.4.2] is Q-factorial. Therefore, it is harmless to add
         the assumption that X is Q-factorial to [Fu5, Lemma 2.4.5].
       • Lemma 2.4.9 in [Fu5] is not correct. There exists a counterexample (see
         [Le, Theorem 1]). For the details, see also [Fu7]. This mistake aﬀects
         Remark 4.11.6 in [Fu5]. Fortunately, it was rescued by [Fu7, Theorem
         3.2].
We correct some typos in [Fu5].
       • On page 172, line 2,
                                       X n
                                           di D i
                                       i=1
         should be replaced by
                                       X
                                       r
                                             di D i .
                                       i=1
       • On page 227, line 10, X ′ = f (Y ′ ) should be replaced by f (Y ′ ). In general,
         X ′ = f (Y ′ ) does not always hold.
       • On page 237, line 22,
                             π∗ OX (mL)) → π∗ OX ′ (mL)
         should be replaced by
                             π∗ OX (mL) → π∗ OX ′ (mL).
       • On page 245, line 17, z, z ′ ∈ F should be replaced by z, z ′ ∈ N E(X/S).
